key_features.classic_presentation: Acute diverticulitis presents with LEFT LOWER QUADRANT (LLQ) PAIN that is CONSTANT and LOCALIZED (unlike right-sided appendicitis). Pain is 6-9/10 severity, aching or sharp. Onset is usually within 1-3 days (subacute). Occurs almost exclusively in patients >40 years old (very rare in young adults). Key associated symptoms: LOW-GRADE FEVER (100-101°F), change in bowel habits (DIARRHEA or constipation), nausea, anorexia. Location: LLQ tenderness, sometimes palpable tender mass. Key history: Known diverticulosis, low-fiber diet, prior episodes. Key positives: LLQ tenderness worse with movement, fever, elevated WBC. Key negatives: Right-sided pain suggests appendicitis. High fever >102°F suggests complicated diverticulitis (abscess, perforation). Profuse diarrhea suggests gastroenteritis. Age <40 makes diverticulitis unlikely.

red_flags: Severe LLQ pain with high fever >102°F and rigors - diverticular abscess, needs CT and possible drainage
Sudden severe pain with peritoneal signs - perforation with peritonitis, call 911
Unable to tolerate oral intake with vomiting - possible obstruction from inflammation
Immunocompromised patients - higher risk of perforation and sepsis
